title: How do you turn facts into insights in a case interview?
description: How to move from describing numbers to explaining what they mean for the client, with a simple three-step habit and examples.
hook: One of the clearest differences between an average and a strong candidate is a two-word question they ask themselves constantly: so what? Average candidates report facts. Strong candidates say what the facts mean for the client. It is a habit, and you can build it.
body:
Fact, insight, implication

  • Fact: "Online sales grew 40%."
  • Insight: "Online is now a quarter of all sales, and it is growing much faster than stores."
  • Implication: "So the client's plan to open 20 new stores may be investing in the slower channel. I'd like to compare the return on new stores with investing in online."

Most candidates stop at the fact. Getting to the implication is where the marks are.

Three questions to ask yourself

  1. Is this big or small compared with something? (last year, competitors, the goal)
  2. What does it explain, or rule out?
  3. What should the client do differently because of it?

After every calculation

Never leave a number hanging. "The break-even is 20,000 units" becomes "The break-even is 20,000 units, which is about 10% of the market. That seems achievable given our current share is 15%."

Practise it anywhere

When you read a news story about a company, ask: so what for them? A supermarket's prices rising faster than inflation: so what? Shoppers might switch to discounters. So what? The supermarket may need to invest in its own-label range. A few minutes of this each day trains exactly the reflex interviewers look for.
outro: Next in this topic: What should you say at each stage of a case interview?
